title: 2 Chronicles 8:1–11
context: 2 Chronicles 8:1–11 gathers notices about Solomon’s building and administration after twenty years of work on the temple and palace. He builds cities that Huram had given him, conquers Hamath Zobah, builds Tadmor and storage cities, fortifies Upper and Lower Beth Horon, and builds wherever he desires. He conscripts the remaining Canaanite peoples for forced labor, while Israelites serve as soldiers and officers. He moves Pharaoh’s daughter out of David’s city, because places where the ark has been are holy. The parallel in 1 Kings 9:10–24 differs in several useful ways, which these notes name without harmonizing. Kings says that Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities, while 8:2 speaks of cities Huram gave to Solomon; Kings gives five hundred fifty chief officers where Chronicles gives two hundred fifty; and Chronicles does not include the Cabul episode or Pharaoh’s capture of Gezer. Both traditions read the passage as a record of Solomon’s prosperity and organization under God’s blessing.

verses.text: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the LORD’s house and his own house,
verses.arminianNotes: At the end of twenty years of building the LORD’s house and his own house, Solomon turns to other projects. Arminian readers see the period of building completed and a new phase of Solomon’s reign beginning, as in 1 Kings 9:10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s blessing in the completion of the work. Both traditions read the verse as a transition to the notices of Solomon’s further building and administration.

verses.text: Solomon built the cities which Huram had given to Solomon, and caused the children of Israel to dwell there.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon builds the cities Huram had given him and settles Israelites there. Arminians note that 1 Kings 9:11–13 says Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities, and they name the difference without trying to harmonize it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and likewise leave the difference as it stands, as the drafted notes on 1 Kings 9 also do. Both traditions read the verse as a record of Solomon’s development of his territory.

verses.text: Solomon went to Hamath Zobah, and prevailed against it.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon goes to Hamath Zobah and prevails against it. Arminian readers note that this campaign is not recorded in 1 Kings, and they read it as part of the Chronicler’s picture of Solomon’s strong kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s blessing in Solomon’s success. Both traditions note that the location of Hamath Zobah is uncertain, and they avoid claiming more than the text gives.

verses.text: He built Tadmor in the wilderness, and all the storage cities, which he built in Hamath.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon builds Tadmor in the wilderness and storage cities in Hamath. Arminians note that 1 Kings 9:18 has Tamar where Chronicles has Tadmor, and they name the difference without resolving it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and leave the difference unharmonized. Tadmor is often identified with the later city of Palmyra, though both traditions hold that identification with caution, and they read the verse as part of Solomon’s building program.

verses.text: Also he built Beth Horon the upper and Beth Horon the lower, fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars;
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon builds Upper and Lower Beth Horon as fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars. Arminian readers see wise defense of a key route into the hill country, a sign of careful government.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the fortifications as part of God’s blessing of security in Solomon’s reign. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 9:17, which mentions Lower Beth Horon.

verses.text: and Baalath, and all the storage cities that Solomon had, and all the cities for his chariots, the cities for his horsemen, and all that Solomon desired to build for his pleasure in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon builds Baalath, storage cities, chariot cities, and whatever he desires in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and his land. Arminians see the breadth of Solomon’s projects as a sign of prosperity, while noting the phrase about his desire.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a description of a prosperous reign. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 9:19 and read the verse without supplying a judgment the text does not make here.

verses.text: As for all the people who were left of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of Israel—
verses.arminianNotes: The verse names the remaining peoples who were not of Israel: Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. Arminian readers see a reminder that Israel had not fully driven out the peoples of the land, as recorded in Judges 1.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as historical background for the forced labor. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 9:20 and treat the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: of their children who were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel didn’t consume—of them Solomon conscripted forced labor to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon conscripts their descendants for forced labor. Arminians read the verse as a historical notice, and they note that the text reports the practice without commenting on it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and also refrain from adding a judgment the text does not make. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 9:21 and read the verse soberly as part of the record of Solomon’s administration.

verses.text: But of the children of Israel, Solomon made no servants for his work, but they were men of war, chief of his captains, and rulers of his chariots and of his horsemen.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon makes no Israelites servants for his work; they serve as soldiers, captains, and chariot officers. Arminian readers note the distinction the text makes, and they also recall that 1 Kings 5:13 and 1 Kings 12:4 speak of burdens laid on Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the tension by reference without harmonizing it. Both traditions read the verse as part of the Chronicler’s summary of Solomon’s administration, consistent with 1 Kings 9:22.

verses.text: These were the chief officers of King Solomon, even two-hundred fifty, who ruled over the people.
verses.arminianNotes: There are two hundred fifty chief officers who rule over the people. Arminians note that 1 Kings 9:23 gives five hundred fifty, and they name the difference without trying to resolve it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and leave the numbers as they stand. Both traditions read the verse as a detail of Solomon’s administration, and they avoid speculation about how the figures were counted.

verses.text: Solomon brought up Pharaoh’s daughter out of David’s city to the house that he had built for her; for he said, “My wife shall not dwell in the house of David king of Israel, because the places where the LORD’s ark has come are holy.”
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon moves Pharaoh’s daughter out of David’s city, saying his wife should not live there because places where the ark has been are holy. Arminian readers see Solomon showing respect for the holiness of the ark’s resting place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that only Chronicles gives this reason, while 1 Kings 9:24 records the move without it. Both traditions read the verse as concern for holiness, and they do not supply here the later warnings about foreign wives found in 1 Kings 11.
